blocks.text: Adapter merging mathematically folds a trained LoRA adapter, covered in earlier modules, permanently into the base model weights, producing a single standalone model that behaves identically to the adapted version but no longer needs the separate adapter loading covered in the previous topic.

This topic covers exactly how the merge computation works, when merging is the right deployment choice over keeping an adapter loaded separately, and the practical consideration of merging more than one adapter together.
1. What Adapter Merging Does

blocks.alt: Base model weights and adapter weights combine into merged weights

blocks.text: Adapter merging computes a new set of model weights by mathematically combining the original base model weights with the trained LoRA adapter contribution, the resulting merged weights produce identical outputs to running the base model with the adapter loaded separately, but as a single unified weight set.
2. Loaded Flexibility vs Merged Simplicity

blocks.alt: Loaded adapter serving offers runtime flexibility while merged adapter serving offers simplicity

blocks.text: This is the same tradeoff introduced from the loading side in the previous Adapter Loading topic, merging gives up the ability to swap adapters at runtime in exchange for a simpler deployment artifact, a single standard model with no extra serving infrastructure needed to manage separate adapter weights.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Choice","Best Fit"],"rows":[["Keep loaded","Multiple tasks or tenants sharing one base model"],["Merge","One fixed task behavior, simplest possible deployment"]]}

blocks.text: 3. The Merge Computation

blocks.alt: LoRA matrix A and matrix B combine into a low rank update added to the base weights

blocks.text: Recalling the LoRA mechanics covered in an earlier module, the adapter represents a low-rank update computed from two smaller matrices, merging multiplies these matrices together to reconstruct a full-sized weight update and adds it directly to the corresponding base model weight matrix, after which the adapter matrices themselves are no longer needed.

code.content:
from peft import PeftModel

model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, "path/to/adapter")
merged_model = model.merge_and_unload()
merged_model.save_pretrained("./merged-model")

blocks.text: 4. Merged vs Unmerged Inference Performance

blocks.alt: Merged model inference is compared against unmerged adapter inference

blocks.text: A merged model runs inference exactly like any standard model with no adapter-related computation overhead at all, an unmerged, loaded adapter setup, covered in the previous topic, adds a small amount of extra computation at inference time to apply the adapter, merging is generally the fastest possible inference path when only one fixed adapter behavior is needed.

blocks.title: This overhead is usually small but not always negligible
blocks.content: For very high throughput serving where every millisecond matters, the small inference overhead of an unmerged adapter can add up, merging removes this overhead entirely at the cost of losing runtime flexibility.

blocks.text: 5. Merging Multiple Adapters Together

blocks.alt: Adapter A and adapter B combine through a weighted combination into a multi-adapter merge

blocks.text: It is possible to merge more than one trained adapter together, combining their weight updates, often with a weighting factor controlling how much each contributes, letting a single merged model blend behaviors learned from separately trained adapters, though the resulting quality depends heavily on how compatible the underlying adapters actually are.
6. Exporting a Merged Model for Deployment

blocks.alt: A merged model exports to a standard deployment format

blocks.text: Once merged, a model can be saved and exported using the standard Hugging Face format, covered in the earlier Transformers topic, or converted further for a specific serving framework, covered in the following vLLM, Ollama, TensorRT-LLM, and TGI topics, without carrying any PEFT-specific dependency forward.
7. The Irreversibility of Merging

blocks.alt: Merging once is compared against keeping the adapter reversible and loaded

blocks.text: Merging is effectively a one-way operation for deployment purposes, once merged, isolating and removing just the adapter contribution from the combined weights is not a practical operation, teams that anticipate needing to update, remove, or swap an adapter later should keep an unmerged copy of the base model and adapter available even if they deploy a merged version.
8. When to Merge in a Fine-Tuning Pipeline

Merging typically happens as a final step after training and evaluation are complete, converting a validated adapter into its simplest deployable form, doing this too early, before confirming the adapter actually performs well, wastes the flexibility that keeping training and adapter artifacts separate would have preserved.
9. Merging Alongside Quantization

Merging is often combined with the quantization techniques covered in an earlier module, producing a merged, quantized model that is both simple to deploy and efficient to run, the order of these operations matters, and following established guidance for the specific quantization method being used avoids introducing unnecessary accuracy loss.
Worked Example

A team finishes fine-tuning and evaluating a LoRA adapter for a single, fixed customer support use case with no plans to swap in other behaviors for this particular deployment. They merge the adapter into the base model using merge_and_unload, producing a standalone model.

This merged model deploys through their standard serving pipeline with zero adapter-related runtime overhead and no dependency on PEFT infrastructure in production, while the team keeps the original unmerged adapter and base model checkpoint archived separately in case they need to retrain or adjust the adapter later.
Common Mistakes

items: Merging an adapter before confirming through evaluation that it actually performs well
Discarding the unmerged adapter and base model after merging, losing the ability to retrain or adjust later
Merging when the actual deployment needs runtime flexibility to swap between multiple adapters
Merging multiple adapters together without checking whether their combined behavior is actually coherent

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuning project you have designed or are familiar with, decide whether the final deployment should merge the adapter or keep it loaded separately, using the tradeoffs covered in this topic and the previous Adapter Loading topic, and justify your choice based on whether the deployment needs to support more than one task behavior.
Key Takeaway

Adapter merging mathematically combines a trained LoRA adapter into the base model weights, producing a standalone model with zero runtime adapter overhead at the cost of losing the flexibility to swap adapters that the loading approach covered in the previous topic preserves, and because merging is effectively irreversible for deployment purposes, it is best done only after an adapter has been fully validated and only when the deployment genuinely needs just one fixed behavior.
